_about: The Grammar tab of the Reference page, for a browser that is not Italian. Each topic: an English intro that explains the concept on English sentences (gr-enx lines), then one point per section with its official-question examples RIGHT AFTER it and an `after` sentence that points at the form in the example just shown, then a recap table last. Every example is a statement of the bank quoted by NUMBER: the app prints its italian_text and english_translation, so an example can never drift from the bank, and validate_data.py fails on a number that is not a live VERO statement or a `hl` that does not occur in it. `hl` is the run of words to mark, matched case-insensitively.

topics.title: Taking a statement apart
topics.intro:
An English reader finds the parts of a sentence largely by where they sit. The subject comes first, the verb follows it, and a comma marks anything that comes before them or interrupts them. The Ministry's statements follow none of these habits reliably, so a statement in which every word is familiar can still be hard to follow.

Three differences cause most of the trouble. The subject often comes after the verb, or is not written at all. Long phrases pile up before the main verb, and nothing marks where they end. Descriptions attach to a noun after it, sometimes several in a row, so a noun and its verb can sit far apart.

Here is a short statement as the Ministry prints it (24843):

Nei farmaci sedativi sono presenti alcune sostanze che possono compromettere la facoltà di guida

Taken apart, it has four parts:

SettingNei farmaci sedativiIn sedative medications
Main verbsono presentiare present
Subjectalcune sostanzesome substances
Which onesche possono compromettere la facoltà di guidathat can impair the ability to drive

An English reader takes farmaci sedativi as the subject, because it comes first. It cannot be the subject, because it sits after the preposition nei. The subject is alcune sostanze, and it comes after the verb.

A long statement combines several of these difficulties at once (24007):

La limitata visuale offerta dal parabrezza degli autocarri nella zona immediatamente antistante il veicolo rende pericolosa la fermata di tali mezzi in colonna, qualora siano presenti pedoni o mezzi a due ruote

Taken apart, it has six parts:

SubjectLa limitata visualeThe limited view
Which viewofferta dal parabrezza degli autocarrioffered by the windshield of trucks
Wherenella zona immediatamente antistante il veicoloin the area immediately in front of the vehicle
Main verbrende pericolosamakes dangerous
Whatla fermata di tali mezzi in colonnastopping such vehicles in a line of traffic
Whenqualora siano presenti pedoni o mezzi a due ruoteif pedestrians or two-wheeled vehicles are present

The main verb is the fifteenth word. Everything before it is the subject and the two descriptions attached to it, offerta and antistante. After the verb, the adjective pericolosa comes before the noun it describes, tali mezzi points back to the trucks, and at the end the subject pedoni again follows its verb. Once the statement is taken apart, the rule is simple: a truck's windshield hides the area just in front of it, so stopping trucks in a line is dangerous when pedestrians or two-wheeled vehicles are nearby.

The missing comma is the difference an English reader usually notices first. English puts a comma after a long opening phrase and after an opening -ing phrase. Italian leaves that comma to the writer, and most statements leave it out. Even after an opening se or quando, where Italian normally does use one, a quarter of the statements in the Ministry test bank do not.

The way through is to find the MAIN VERB first. Everything before it is either the subject or a phrase that sets the scene, and the words after it complete the sentence. In each line below the main verb is in bold:

Su strade coperte di neve occorre evitare brusche manovre. On snow-covered roads you must avoid abrupt maneuvers.
Il conducente che intende sorpassare deve accertarsi… The driver who intends to pass must make sure…
Nelle aree pedonali possono transitare le biciclette. Bicycles may go through pedestrian areas.

In the first line the subject is left out, because it is you. In the third the subject comes after the verb. The main verb is most often a duty or permission word (è vietato, bisogna, deve, può) or the verb that says what a sign does (indica, preannuncia). The points below show the shapes that hide the verb or its subject most often.

sections.h: A phrase that sets the scene: in presenza del segnale, su strade, nelle aree, per svoltare
sections.p: Many statements open with a phrase that says where, or in what situation, the rule applies, and no comma follows it. The phrase ends just before the first verb, which is most often è, bisogna, occorre, deve or si. Two such phrases can follow each other, and the second often opens with per, meaning in order to.
sections.after: In the first, occorre is the main verb, so su strade coperte di neve is the setting. In the second, two phrases come before bisogna: where (su strada a senso unico) and what for (per svoltare a sinistra).

sections.h: The subject after the verb: è vietato il, è consentito il, possono circolare i
sections.p:
In English the subject almost always comes before the verb. The exceptions are a few fixed forms, such as there is a sign or a question, so an English reader takes the first noun as the subject without thinking about it. Italian often puts the subject after the verb, and the statements do it constantly. It happens after è with a word such as vietato, consentito or obbligatorio, and after verbs of movement or change such as circolare, transitare or aumentare.

Three checks find the subject. First, when the statement opens with a setting or a condition, the nouns inside it belong to that phrase and are not the subject of the main verb. Second, when the main verb is followed by an article and a noun, that noun is probably the subject. Third, check the agreement: a plural verb needs a plural subject, and vietata needs a feminine one, so the noun that fits is the subject.

ex.hl: possono circolare solo i veicoli autorizzati

sections.after: È vietato il trasporto di minori: the transport of minors is prohibited, and il trasporto is the subject. Possono circolare solo i veicoli autorizzati: only authorized vehicles may travel. I veicoli is the subject of possono, which is why the verb is plural.

sections.h: No subject written: dobbiamo, abbiamo, possiamo, ci, bisogna, occorre
sections.p:
English always writes its subject, even when it is only it or you. Italian leaves it out when the verb's ending already says who, so a statement can have no subject word at all. In the statements the missing subject is nearly always you, the driver, and it shows up in three ways.

A verb ending in -iamo, such as dobbiamo, abbiamo or possiamo, means we, and ci in front of a verb means us. Both refer to the driver reading the statement. Bisogna, occorre and è vietato followed by an infinitive name nobody, and English supplies you must or it is forbidden to. A second verb joined by e or ma keeps the subject of the first.
sections.after: In the first, dobbiamo is we must, and in ci diano la precedenza the ci is us: the other vehicles yield to you. In the second, bisogna pulire has no subject at all, and the English supplies you must clean.

sections.h: A pronoun on the end of the verb: mettersi, fermarsi, bloccarglieli
sections.p: Italian attaches small pronouns to the END of an infinitive, where an English reader, looking at the verb, easily skips them. Those endings say who or what the action is about. -si means oneself, the person doing the action, which in the statements is the driver. -lo, -la, -li and -le mean it or them, a thing already named. -gli means to him or for him. Before you decide what the verb is about, read its ending.

ex.hl: evitare di mettersi sotto il veicolo

sections.after: In the first, mettersi is mettere + si, to put oneself: it is you who must not go under the car, not the jack. In the second, bloccarglieli is bloccare + gli + li, to immobilize them (the limbs) for him (the injured person).

sections.h: Two negative words, one negation: non ... mai, non ... né
sections.p: Italian often puts non in front of the verb and a second negative word after it: non ... mai (never), non ... né ... né (neither ... nor), non ... nessuno (nobody), non ... niente (nothing). In English two negatives cancel out or sound wrong; in Italian they do not cancel. The pair is ONE negation, and the second word says what kind.

ex.hl: non guardare né a destra, né a sinistra

sections.after: Non deve mai sopravvalutare: must never overestimate, not must not never. Non guardare né a destra, né a sinistra: look neither right nor left. So non bisogna mai means you must never, a ban with no exception.

sections.h: A condition that sets the scene: quando, se
sections.p: A clause that opens with quando or se has a verb of its own, so the first verb in the statement is not the main one. The condition ends where a second verb begins. An English sentence puts a comma there.

ex.hl: Quando si incontrano le strisce di figura dipinte sulla pavimentazione

sections.after: In the first, si incontrano belongs to the condition and occorre is the main verb. In the second, si traina belongs to the condition and aumenta is the main verb, with its subject after it: the braking distance increases.

sections.h: A gerund that sets the scene: giungendo, percorrendo, dovendo, incontrando
sections.p: A verb ending in -ando or -endo at the start of a statement means when or while doing something. The words after it complete that action, and the main verb comes after them. The one doing the action is you, or the vehicle named right after the phrase.

ex.hl: Giungendo in vicinanza di un incrocio

sections.after: In the first, giungendo in vicinanza di un incrocio means when you approach an intersection, and bisogna is the main verb. In the second, the phrase ends at in figura. Il veicolo D is the one arriving, and it is also the subject of the main verb deve.

sections.h: A subject with a che clause inside it: il conducente che
sections.p: When the subject is followed by che and a verb, that clause describes the subject and belongs to it. The subject runs on until a second verb arrives, usually deve, può, è or non with a verb. That second verb is the main one.

ex.hl: Il conducente che intende fermarsi sul margine destro della carreggiata
Il conducente che partecipa a gare di velocità non autorizzate su aree pubbliche

sections.after: In the first, the subject ends at carreggiata and deve segnalare is the main verb. In the second, it ends at pubbliche and è punito is the main verb: the driver who takes part in such races is punished.

sections.h: Two kinds of che: indica che, veicoli che
sections.p: After a verb of saying or checking, such as indica, preannuncia or accertarsi, che means that and opens what is said or checked. After a noun, che means who or which and describes that noun. One statement often holds both.

ex.hl: sui veicoli che si immettono da destra

sections.after: In the first, indica che opens what the sign says, and the later ciclisti che attraversano is a description: cyclists who cross. In the second, the marked che follows the noun veicoli, so it means which: vehicles which merge from the right.

sections.h: A description after a noun, without che: provenienti da, adibiti al, posto in
sections.p: A word ending in -ante or -ente (proveniente, circolante), or a past participle (posto, adibito, destinato, munito), placed after a noun describes that noun. The phrase after it belongs to the description. Read it as which is or which are. It is never the main verb.

ex.hl: veicoli adibiti al trasporto di cose

sections.after: I veicoli provenienti da destra: the vehicles which come from the right. I veicoli adibiti al trasporto di cose: the vehicles which are used to carry goods. The verbs that govern them are elsewhere, ha in the first and vieta in the second.

sections.h: A chain of di: di, del, della, dei, degli
sections.p: Italian builds long noun phrases by joining nouns with di and its forms. Each di attaches to the noun just before it, so the chain is read from left to right, one link at a time. The whole chain is a single noun phrase, and its first noun is the one the sentence is about.

ex.hl: Lo spessore minimo del battistrada degli pneumatici di un autoveicolo

sections.after: The minimum thickness, of the tread, of the tires, of a motor vehicle. Lo spessore is the subject, and deve essere is its verb.

sections.h: An infinitive as the subject: spostare, trainare, viaggiare
sections.p: A statement that opens with an infinitive names an action and then says something about it. The infinitive and the words it governs form the subject, and the main verb comes later, often è, può or a verb such as comporta. In English the infinitive becomes a word ending in -ing.

ex.hl: Trainare un rimorchio su strade con forti salite

sections.after: Spostare la segnaletica stradale means moving road signs, and può comportare is the main verb. Trainare un rimorchio su strade con forti salite means towing a trailer on steep roads, and fa aumentare is the main verb.

sections.h: Words that point back: ciò, esso, essa, vi, ne
sections.p: A few short words stand for something already named. Ciò means this or that and refers to an action just mentioned. Esso and essa mean it and refer to a thing. Vi means there, as in vi è, there is. Ne means of it or with it. Find the noun such a word refers to before reading on.

ex.hl: se il veicolo ne è provvisto

sections.after: Ne è provvisto means is fitted with it, and ne stands for la doppia trazione, the all-wheel drive. In di essa, essa stands for la carreggiata, the feminine noun named earlier in the statement.

rows: in presenza di…, su strade…, per svoltare…
the setting ends at the first verb
è vietato il…, possono circolare i…
no subject word; it is you, the driver
the ending says who or what: -si oneself, -lo/-li it or them, -gli to him
the main verb is the second verb
the main verb comes after the gerund and its words
the main verb follows the che clause

topics.title: Linking words: qualora, purché, allorché, in attesa che, in quanto
topics.intro:
Many statements have two parts: a main part that states the rule, and a second part that says when, on what condition, for what purpose or for what reason the rule applies. A linking word opens the second part. In English these are words such as if, provided that, while, so that and because:

Rallenta qualora piova. Slow down if it rains.
Puoi passare purché la strada sia libera. You may go provided that the road is clear.
Resta in auto in attesa che arrivi l'agente. Stay in the car until the officer arrives.

Two things make these words hard for an English reader. Several of them are formal words that are rare outside legal and official Italian, such as qualora, ove and allorché, so a B1 reader may never have met them. And many of them are followed by the subjunctive (sia, piova, arrivi, venga). The subjunctive is a useful signal: it tells you that the second part describes a condition or a possibility, not a fact that is already true.

If you miss the linking word, you read the condition as part of the rule, and the statement seems to say something it does not say. Each point below takes one linking word or one small group.

sections.h: A condition: qualora
sections.p: Qualora means if or in case. It is formal and is followed by the subjunctive. Read it exactly as se.
sections.after: Qualora sia difficile: if it is difficult. Sia is the subjunctive of essere, which is why it follows qualora.

sections.h: A condition: purché
sections.p: Purché means provided that or as long as. The main part is allowed or required only when the condition after purché is met. It takes the subjunctive, and sometimes it is followed by a participle with no verb at all.
sections.after: Purché lo si possa fare: provided that one can do so; possa is the subjunctive of potere. Purché custoditi: provided that they are kept, with siano left out.

sections.h: A condition: nel caso in cui
sections.p: Nel caso in cui means in the event that or simply if. It usually takes the subjunctive.

ex.hl: nel caso in cui non funzionino

sections.after: Nel caso in cui non funzionino: in the event that they do not work; funzionino is the subjunctive of funzionare. In the second example the subjunctive is venga rubato, is stolen.

sections.h: An exception: salvo che
sections.p: Salvo che means unless or except when. It removes some cases from the rule stated before it. A non after salvo che adds nothing and is not a negation.
sections.after: Salvo che si tratti di veicoli a due ruote: unless they are two-wheeled vehicles. Salvo che non sia esentato means unless he is exempt, not unless he is not exempt.

sections.h: Where, or if: ove
sections.p: Ove is a formal word for where, and it can also mean if or when. It is not a misspelling of dove.
sections.after: Ove possibile: where possible. Ove non esista marciapiede rialzato: where there is no raised sidewalk; esista is the subjunctive of esistere.

sections.h: A time: allorché
sections.p: Allorché is a formal word for when. It sets the moment at which the rule applies, often at the very start of the statement.
sections.after: Allorché di notte ... incrociamo: when at night we meet. The verb comes several words later, after the setting di notte, su strada extraurbana. Allorché vengano violate: when (rules) are violated.

sections.h: A time: in attesa che
sections.p: In attesa che means while waiting for something to happen, or until it happens. It is built on attesa, the wait, and it takes the subjunctive. The main part describes what you do during the wait.
sections.after: In attesa che arrivi il soccorso medico: while waiting for medical help to arrive. Arrivi and arrivino are the subjunctive of arrivare, singular and plural.

sections.h: A time: prima che, finché
sections.p: Prima che means before something happens and takes the subjunctive. Finché means as long as or until, depending on the verb after it.
sections.after: Prima che si abbassi la semibarriera: before the half-barrier comes down. Finché le strisce sono ancora discontinue: as long as the lines are still broken.

sections.h: A purpose: in modo da, in modo che, affinché
sections.p: These say what the action is for. In modo da is followed by an infinitive and means so as to. In modo che and affinché are followed by the subjunctive and mean so that.

ex.hl: in modo che sia ben visibile

sections.after: In modo da evitarne la caduta: so as to prevent it from falling. In modo che sia ben visibile: so that it is clearly visible; sia is the subjunctive.

sections.h: A reason: in quanto, poiché
sections.p: In quanto and poiché both mean because or since. In quanto does not mean in how much. When poiché opens the statement, the reason comes first and the rule follows.
sections.after: In quanto costituisce pericolo: because it constitutes a danger. Poiché la marcia dei ciclisti ...: since cyclists ..., and the rule begins at il conducente.

sections.h: Even if: anche se
sections.p: Anche se means even if or even though. It says that the rule still applies in the case it names. It can be followed by a full verb or by an adjective alone.
sections.after: Anche se non sono consumati: even if they are not worn. Anche se maggiorenne: even if an adult, with è left out.

rows: if, in the event that (+ subjunctive)
unless; a non after it is not a negation
before (+ subjunctive); as long as, until
in modo da, in modo che, affinché
so as to (+ infinitive); so that (+ subjunctive)

topics.title: andare and venire in front of a past participle
topics.intro:
You know the passive with essere. Two other verbs take its place in front of the same participle, and neither means what it means on its own: andare is not going and venire is not coming.

Il negozio è chiuso. The store is closed.
Il negozio va chiuso. The store must be closed.
Il negozio viene chiuso. The store is being closed.

The participle is the same word in all three, and it agrees with the subject as it does after essere.

sections.h: andare: what must be done
sections.p: Andare + participle states an obligation and has nothing to do with going. Read va as must be, vanno as the plural. It belongs with the duty words too, and the duty topic sets it against dovere.
sections.after: Va diminuita: must be reduced. Non va effettuata: must not be performed; the negative goes in front.

sections.h: venire: something is being done to the subject
sections.p: È chiuso can mean two things: the store is in a closed state, or somebody is closing it. Venire + participle keeps only the second: something is happening to the subject, and somebody else is doing it. Read viene as is being or gets.
sections.after: Il veicolo che viene sorpassato: the vehicle that is being overtaken, by another driver. Se si viene sorpassati: if you are being overtaken; the si makes it you, and the participle goes plural after si.

sections.h: venire where English says a plain is
sections.p: The questions use venire where English is content with is, because the sentence is about the act of placing, not the state of standing there. Viene posto and è posto both translate as is placed.
sections.after: Viene for a singular subject, vengono for a plural one: posto, posti.

sections.h: One venire phrase to know
sections.p: The venire passive the questions use most is about the license.
sections.after: La patente viene ritirata: the license is withdrawn, by the police. The adverb between the two words does not break the pair.

rows: a state, or the plain passive

topics.title: Who is doing it to whom: sorpassa, sorpassato, precede, segue
topics.intro:
Many statements name two vehicles, and the answer turns on which one you are. Italian marks the one acting and the one acted on by the shape of the phrase, not by word order:

Il veicolo che sorpassa. The vehicle that is passing.
Il veicolo sorpassato. The vehicle being passed.
Il veicolo che precede. The vehicle ahead.
Il veicolo che segue. The vehicle behind.

Read the verb form before deciding which vehicle you are.

sections.h: The one acting: che + a verb
sections.p: Che followed by a verb in an ordinary tense names the one doing the action. Il conducente che intende sorpassare is the driver about to pass; il veicolo che sorpassa is the one passing.
sections.after: Both intende and sorpassa are active verbs, so both name the vehicle doing the passing.

sections.h: The one acted on: sorpassato, da sorpassare
sections.p: The vehicle on the receiving end is named by the past participle alone, il veicolo sorpassato, or by da + infinitive, il veicolo da sorpassare, the vehicle to be passed. Che viene sorpassato says the same thing with venire.
sections.after: Sorpassato and da sorpassare both name the vehicle being passed; the driver who acts is the other one.

sections.h: When it is you: si viene sorpassati, essere tamponati
sections.p: With si or an impersonal verb the subject is you. Si viene sorpassati: you are being passed. Evitare di essere tamponati dal veicolo che segue: you are the one hit, and dal names who hits you.

ex.hl: essere tamponati dal veicolo che segue

sections.after: In both, the other vehicle acts and you receive the action; da or dal in front of a vehicle names the one acting.

sections.h: Ahead and behind: che precede, che segue
sections.p: Il veicolo che precede is the vehicle ahead of you, il veicolo che segue the one behind. When a pronoun sits in between, che lo precede, che lo segue, the lo is your own vehicle.
sections.after: Il veicolo che lo precede: the vehicle that precedes it, that is, ahead of the driver's vehicle. Il conducente che lo segue: the driver behind him.

sections.h: Yielding: dare la precedenza a, avere la precedenza su
sections.p: Dare la precedenza a is to yield to: the vehicle after a goes first. Avere la precedenza su is to have the right of way over: the vehicle after su waits.

ex.hl: ha la precedenza sul veicolo C

sections.after: Dare la precedenza ai ciclisti: the cyclists go first. D ha la precedenza sul veicolo C: D goes first and C waits.

sections.h: Who did it, when the action is a noun: da parte di
sections.p: When the action is written as a noun, l'attraversamento, il traino, the one doing it follows da parte di.
sections.after: L'attraversamento da parte di un bambino: a child does the crossing. Il traino di un veicolo da parte di un altro: the other vehicle does the towing.

rows: sorpassato, da sorpassare, che viene sorpassato

topics.title: The impersonal si: si può, si deve, si trova
topics.intro:
English states a rule without naming anyone in three ways, and Italian covers all three with si before a verb in the third person:

Ci si deve fermare alla linea. You must stop at the line.
Ci si deve fermare alla linea. One must stop at the line.
Il segnale si può trovare sulle autostrade. The sign can be found on autostrade.

It is the most common construction in the official questions. This si is not the reflexive himself and not yes.

sections.h: si + verb: you, one, people in general
sections.p: With no noun as subject, si + singular verb means you or one in general.
sections.after: Si viaggia: you travel. Si intende prendere: you intend to take.

sections.h: si + verb + noun: a passive
sections.p: When a noun follows, the noun is the subject and the verb agrees with it.
sections.after: Il segnale si può trovare: the sign can be found. Si possono richiedere informazioni: information can be requested; plural noun, plural verb.

sections.h: The plural verb is the clue
sections.p: A plural verb after si tells you the noun beside it is the subject.
sections.after: Le strade che si incrociano: the roads that cross.

sections.h: ci si: si with a reflexive verb
sections.p: A reflexive verb already carries si (avvicinarsi, immettersi), and Italian does not write si si. The impersonal one becomes ci.
sections.after: Ci si sta avvicinando: you are approaching. Ci si immette: you merge. This ci is not there.

sections.h: The plural ending after si
sections.p: After the impersonal si a participle or adjective goes into the masculine plural, because the unnamed you counts as more than one person. The verb stays singular.
sections.after: Si è usciti: you have exited. Si è affaticati: you are fatigued. The -i is the rule, not a mistake.

sections.h: The same ending after si rimane
sections.p: Rimanere after si takes the same plural participle.
sections.after: Si rimane bloccati: you are stuck.

sections.h: non si: the negative
sections.p: The negative goes in front of si.
sections.after: Non si incrociano veicoli: no vehicles are encountered. Read the non before deciding what the sentence claims.

rows: the noun is the subject; a passive

topics.title: A duty: va, deve essere, obbligatorio, bisogna, occorre, necessario, si deve, tenuto a
topics.intro:
The questions state a duty with a fixed set of phrases. They all mean must, and differ in how the sentence is built around them:

Il negozio va chiuso. The store must be closed.
Il negozio deve essere chiuso. The store must be closed.
Bisogna chiudere il negozio. You have to close the store.
Il gestore è tenuto a chiudere il negozio. The manager is required to close the store.

The first two put the duty on the thing; the third on nobody in particular; only the last names the person.

sections.h: A duty: va + past participle
sections.p: Andare in front of a past participle states an obligation, and has nothing to do with going. Read va as must be and vanno as the plural; the participle agrees with the subject.
sections.after: Va diminuita: must be reduced. Non va effettuata: must not be performed; the negative goes in front.

sections.h: A duty: deve essere, and dovere with a person
sections.p: Andare + participle says the same thing as deve essere + participle, and the questions use both for the same rule. The difference is only in what the sentence is about: with andare or deve essere the subject is the thing the duty falls on, and nobody is named; with dovere + infinitive the subject is the person who must act.
sections.after: Deve essere rispettato could be written va rispettato with no change of meaning. To name the driver the questions switch to the infinitive: il conducente deve regolare la velocità.

sections.h: A duty: è obbligatorio
sections.p: È obbligatorio is it is mandatory, and it is used two ways. Before an infinitive it is fixed as obbligatorio. As an adjective it agrees with its noun: obbligatoria, obbligatori.
sections.after: È obbligatorio mantenere: it is mandatory to maintain. L'assicurazione è obbligatoria: feminine, because assicurazione is.

sections.h: A duty: bisogna
sections.p: Bisogna is you have to. It never has a subject and never changes form: always bisogna, always an infinitive after it.
sections.after: Bisogna proseguire: you have to continue. Nobody is named; the duty is everybody's.

sections.h: A duty: occorre
sections.p: Occorre is it is necessary, used like bisogna: no subject, an infinitive after it. On its own, se occorre is if need be.
sections.after: Occorre diminuire: it is necessary to reduce.

sections.h: A duty: è necessario
sections.p: È necessario says what occorre says, in two shapes. Before an infinitive it is fixed. As an adjective it agrees with its noun and says what the thing is needed for, with per.
sections.after: È necessario arrestarsi: it is necessary to stop. L'uso è necessario per segnalare: the use is needed to signal.

sections.h: A duty: si deve
sections.p: Si deve is you must, with the impersonal si and an infinitive. When the verb is reflexive, a second pronoun appears: ci si deve.
sections.after: Si deve proseguire: you must continue. Ci si deve spostare: you must move over; the ci is there because spostarsi is reflexive.

sections.h: A duty: è tenuto a
sections.p: È tenuto a is is required to, and unlike the words above it names the person under the duty, so it agrees with that person: è tenuto a, sono tenuti a. An infinitive follows the a.
sections.after: Il conducente è tenuto a evitare: the driver is required to avoid.

topics.title: Advice: opportuno, consigliabile, conviene
topics.intro:
Three phrases say that something is wise, not required. Each takes an infinitive:

È opportuno fermarsi. It is advisable to stop.
È consigliabile fermarsi. It is advisable to stop.
Conviene fermarsi. It is best to stop.

None of them says the Code obliges anyone, which is the difference from a duty.

sections.h: Advice: è opportuno
sections.p: È opportuno is it is advisable: wise, not required. Before an infinitive it is fixed. Before a clause it takes che and the subjunctive.
sections.after: È opportuno mantenere: it is advisable to keep. È opportuno che vi sia: it is advisable that there be; sia is the subjunctive of essere.

sections.h: Advice: è consigliabile
sections.p: È consigliabile is it is advisable, the same strength as è opportuno, with an infinitive after it. Non goes in front of the infinitive, not in front of è.
sections.after: È consigliabile suonare: it is advisable to sound. È consigliabile non avvicinarsi: it is advisable not to get close.

sections.h: Advice: conviene
sections.p: Conviene is it is best to, with an infinitive; here it has nothing to do with convenience. Non conviene is it is best not to.
sections.after: Conviene aumentare: it is best to increase. Non conviene fare uso: it is best not to use.

topics.title: Permission: consentito, si può
topics.intro:
Two phrases grant a permission, and a permission is not a duty:

È consentita la sosta. Parking is permitted.
È consentito sostare. It is permitted to park.
Si può sostare. You may park.

Consentito agrees with a noun and stays fixed before an infinitive; si può takes an infinitive.

sections.h: Permission: è consentito
sections.p: È consentito is it is permitted, used two ways. Before a noun it agrees with the noun: è consentito il campeggio, è consentita la sosta. Before an infinitive it stays consentito.
sections.after: È consentito il campeggio: camping is permitted. È consentito sorpassare: it is permitted to overtake.

sections.h: Permission: si può
sections.p: Si può is you may or can be, with an infinitive. When the thing that can be done is plural, the verb goes plural: si possono.
sections.after: Il segnale si può trovare: the sign can be found. Le luci si possono trovare: the lights can be found; plural luci, plural possono.

rows: agrees with a noun; fixed before an infinitive
+ infinitive; plural with a plural thing

topics.title: A ban: vietato, non è consentito, non si può
topics.intro:
A ban is written with vietato or by negating a permission:

È vietata la sosta. Parking is prohibited.
È vietato sostare. It is forbidden to park.
Non si può sostare. You may not park.

Vietato behaves exactly like consentito: it agrees with a noun and stays fixed before an infinitive.

sections.h: A ban: è vietato
sections.p: È vietato is it is forbidden, and it works like consentito: it agrees with a noun and stays fixed before an infinitive.
sections.after: È vietata l'inversione: feminine, because inversione is. È vietato superare: it is forbidden to exceed.

sections.h: A ban: non è consentito, non si può
sections.p: The two permission forms say a ban from the other side: non è consentito is it is not permitted, non si può is you may not.
sections.after: Non è consentito sostare: it is not permitted to park. Non si può proseguire: you may not continue.
